result.topic_en: Euler derives, from the observed mid-eclipse quantities, a small-angle formula for the time correction to add to the middle of a lunar eclipse to get the moment of true opposition, and the corresponding longitude of the Moon and the shadow's centre.
result.transcription:
374 L. EULERI OPERA POSTHUMA.
Cum autem anguli $c$, $z(m+k)$, et $z(n+k)$ sint minimi, eorum tangentes ipsis angulis in [?]
radii $=1$ conversis aequantur, quae conversio fit angulos per $g=0{,}0000048481$ multiplic[?]
unde fiet
$$\frac{\cos\varrho\,(\operatorname{tang}x+gz(n+k)-cg)}{1-g(z(n+k)-c)\operatorname{tang}x}=\frac{\operatorname{tang}x+gz(m+k)}{1-gz(m+k)\operatorname{tang}x}$$
seu $\cos\varrho\operatorname{tang}x+gz(n+k)\cos\varrho-cg\cos\varrho-gz(m+k)\cos\varrho\operatorname{tang}^2x=$
$\operatorname{tang}x+gz(m+k)-g(z(n+k)-c)\operatorname{tang}^2x$,
hincque eruitur
$$gz=\frac{(1-\cos\varrho)\operatorname{tang}x+gc\operatorname{tang}^2x+gc\cos\varrho}{(n+k)\cos\varrho-(m+k)\cos\varrho\operatorname{tang}^2x-(m+k)+(n+k)\operatorname{tang}^2x}$$
seu $$gz=\frac{(1-\cos\varrho)\sin x\cos x+gc\sin^2x+gc\cos\varrho\cos^2x}{(n+k)\cos\varrho\cos^2x-(m+k)\cos\varrho\sin^2x-(m+k)\cos^2x+(n+k)\sin^2x}$$
§ 23. Quia vero est $\sin x\cos x=\tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x$, $\sin^2x=\tfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos 2x)$ et $\cos^2x=\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\cos 2x)$
erit $$gz=\frac{(1-\cos\varrho)\sin 2x+gc-gc\cos 2x+gc\cos\varrho+gc\cos\varrho\cos 2x}{(n+k)(1+\cos\varrho)-(n+k)\cos 2x(1-\cos\varrho)-(m+k)(1+\cos\varrho)-(m+k)\cos 2x(1-\cos\varrho)}$$
seu ob $1-\cos\varrho=2\sin^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$ et $1+\cos\varrho=2\cos^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$ habebitur
$$gz=\frac{\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho+gc-gc\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho}{n-m-(m+n+2k)\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho}.$$
Cum autem sit $gc=\frac{(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{n-m}$, erit
$$gz=\frac{2(n+k)\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho-(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}^4\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{(n-m)^2-(n-m)(m+n+2k)\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}$$
ideoque proxime $gz=$
$\frac{2(n+k)}{(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho-\frac{(m+n+2k)}{(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}^4\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho+\frac{2(n+k)(m+n+2k)}{(n-m)^3}\sin 2x\cos 2x\operatorname{tang}$[?]
ob terminos autem posteriores minimos erit
$$z=\frac{2(n+k)}{g(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$$
qui numerus indicabit partem horae ad momentum eclipsis medium addendam, ut prodeat momentum
verae oppositionis. Vel ad hoc obtinendum, ad momentum eclipsis medium addantur tot minuta[?]
secunda, quot haec expressio $\frac{7200(n+k)}{g(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$ continet unitates. In vera autem oppositione
tione longitudo tam lunae quam centri umbrae a nodo computata erit
$$x+\frac{2(m+k)(n+k)}{g(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$$
seu si medio eclipsis fuerit longitudo umbrae $=U$, erit in oppositione utraque longitudo
$$=U+\frac{2(m+k)(n+k)}{g(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho\ \text{min. sec.}$$

items.quote:
ob terminos autem posteriores minimos erit
$$z=\frac{2(n+k)}{g(n-m)^2}\sin 2x\operatorname{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$$
items.english: Since the later terms are very small, z = 2(n+k)/(g(n−m)^2) · sin 2x · tan^2(ρ/2).

items.quote: seu si medio eclipsis fuerit longitudo umbrae $=U$, erit in oppositione utraque longitudo
items.english: Or, if at the middle of the eclipse the longitude of the shadow was U, then at opposition both longitudes will be U + 2(m+k)(n+k)/(g(n−m)^2) · sin 2x · tan^2(ρ/2), in seconds.
